- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥ 0.6) over recent days, model tends to under-forecast; adjust forecast upward by 1–3% of recent mean or 2–5 points depending on volatility.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior 5-day avg), model often over-anticipates and overshoots; reduce forecast by 2–5% or 5–10 points in next 5–7 days.
- If model forecast is flat or slowly rising while sentiment is rising, it’s likely missing momentum; increase slope or add 1–2% upward bias.
- When true outcome exceeds forecast by >10% over 3–5 days, model may be under-reacting to sentiment; apply “sentiment-driven correction” — add 0.5–1.5x sentiment magnitude to forecast.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if recent 10-day mean is rising, model often lags; add 1–3% to forecast to catch momentum.
- If sentiment is negative or neutral, model tends to over-forecast; reduce forecast by 1–3% or 2–5 points to align with sentiment.
- If forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 days of decline after peak), reduce forecast slope or add 1–2% downward bias.
- When sentiment is high but price is flat or declining, model may be overconfident; reduce forecast by 1–2% to reflect sentiment divergence.
